utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Traldi, do you think that - I think you have some two and a half hours left - that you will be able to conclude the cross-examination within that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll certainly endeavour to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Chamber was informed that the witness had a strong wish to be able to return home. He has -- because he has commitments tomorrow. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, judging by what I have today, it would be ten minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then perhaps the witness himself could also add to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you'd very much wish to be able to return, if possible today. You have commitments at home. You can certainly contribute to that, to achieving that aim by giving focussed answers on the questions. I think it already went quite a bit better yesterday. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination but not until after I have reminded you that you have still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will stay here in The Hague as long as is necessary to the Court and to the Defence. That's my evidence for you. My other obligations are a different matter. I will stay here as long as you need me. And, of course, I -- I accept your suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. And, nevertheless, we will see whether we can accommodate you. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31857.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an article in Sedam Dana by Slavisa Sabljic titled: Black flags in a village that was sacrificed. Turning to page 2 in the English, in the middle, and at the bottom of the left-hand column in the B/C/S he refers to an attack on Kijevo by members of the JNA, territorials from Knin, and the Krajina policemen, on the one hand, and the MUP of the Republic of Croatia and the National Guard Corps on the other. And then turning to page 3 in the English, the middle of page 1 in B/C/S, below the picture, he writes: "In fact, Kijevo is a village without any villagers now and no one knows if anyone will ever return there. This was a big village with about 1.000 inhabitants. They were exclusively Croats." Now, you mentioned Kijevo a couple of times in your reports and you criticised Dr. Donia's references to it. The truth is, after the attack, what used to be a Croat village of 1.000 people was empty; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that Croats remained there after the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could not agree with your interpretation of what happened there, but as for the report of Robert Donia, which is discussed here, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'd asked you a simple question. It was empty of its Croat population after the attack; right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of your question, yes; but your interpretation of the event, no. And I said I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31861.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is an article from Belgrade Radio on 26 August, 1991. We see it begins that: "At 1210 at one of numerous firing positions toward Kijevo, we heard the following message: Kijevo no longer exists." That's an accurate reflection of the scale of the destruction of the village; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is whether Kijevo existed after the fighting in Kijevo; right? Whether it was devastated in the measure it is said here. I wasn't there. I can't testify to whether Kijevo still existed or whether it was destroyed to that extent. But, as I said, I would like to have the opportunity to explain, especially about the report of Dr. Donia and what he says about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the report of Dr. Donia was put to you. What was put to you is a newspaper article, it was referred that you criticised Dr. Donia and then Mr. Traldi started asking you about what, as far as you know, what happened in Kijevo. Therefore -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I can say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 31857 and 31861.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 31857 will be Exhibit P7725. And 65 ter 31861 will be Exhibit P7726.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7725 and 7726 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33374.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is an article titled: The Serbian Vukovar shall live, published in a magazine called Velika Srbija in February 1992. Velika Srbija was published by the Serb Radical Party; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The SRS was a Serb nationalist party; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on what you understand by nationalist. These are labels. Somebody can be an imperialist or a nationalist. It all depends. I would not like to go into ideological labelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, sir, the name of the publication, Velika Srbija, that's translated as Greater Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that was part of the goal the accomplishment of Greater Serbia was part of the goal of that party and its president, Vojislav Seselj; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Greater Serbia is an ideal from the 19th and early 20th century --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in that there was nothing contestable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I hadn't asked you who had that goal in the 19th century. I asked you whether a specific person and his political party had that goal in 1992. That's Vojislav Seselj and the SRS. Do you agree that they had that goal in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you define the nationalism, make your question precisely and I will answer it. What is a nationalist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that was one of the previous questions. Would you now answer the present question, whether Greater Serbia was one of the goals of the party led by Mr. Vojislav Seselj. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering that Seselj himself says it was an objective of his party, there is no reason for me to challenge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we begin -- we read at the beginning, the author says: "At the beginning of December, together with a group of volunteers, I visited Vukovar, a city which no longer exists." If we turn to page 4 in English, 3 in B/C/S, the very end of the article --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just have the very end in English. And that will be page 5 - sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We read three paragraphs before the end: "Only the skeletons of buildings were left as a warning sign. The Count and the Nobel prize winner were left homeless. Everybody is Vukovar is homeless." Now again, you criticise Dr. Donia's description of events in Vukovar in your report. You don't contest that this is the scale of the damage that Vukovar experienced; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to confirm whether there was devastation in Vukovar, yes, whether there was fighting, yes. Donia's interpretation, no. Let me just say this. The JNA was attacked in Vukovar. These were defence actions of the Yugoslav People's Army and that goes for Kijevo too. So the JNA was attacked, Vladimir Seks, the president of the Croatian Parliament, announced an attack earlier on the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army. Knowing that is quite enough for you to understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter 33374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P7727, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 20710.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a transcript of an intercepted conversation on the 21st of April 1992 between Goran Saric and Mico Davidovic, members of the Republika Srpska and federal MUPs, respectively. We see on this page they introduce themselves. Turning to page 4 in the English and 2 in the B/C/S - at the bottom in the B/C/S - Saric says: "The town of Sarajevo is well, okay, normally Bijeljina, Zvornik and this part that has been solved, Krajina and that is solved, as well. It is known who owns that." Pausing there for a moment, you agree that Bijeljina, Zvornik and Krajina, that is to say, the ARK were all territories claimed by the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You do not agree that the Serbs claimed Bijeljina, Zvornik and the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll be very interested to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you submitted to the honourable Court the war objectives of the Republika Srpska. Those were strategic objectives and you insisted on them. It says there that Republika Srpska should liberate the Serbian Krajina and Podrinje and connect them with a corridor. It doesn't say exactly there which cities and towns should go to Republika Srpska. On the contrary. From the debates in the Parliament of Republika Srpska one can see that the leadership of Republika Srpska was prepared for an exchange of territories, and I have statements by General Mladic himself. If it is important to the Court, I'll read them out. So you cannot put it this way. The cities claim ready not clearly defined. Boundaries are contested. They will perhaps change during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, now Saric then says, turning to page 3 in the B/C/S and I'll come back to that point in a moment: "However, as for Sarajevo, whether there will be life in it or not, that is a big question that nobody in the world can answer." And then a few lines below: "Well, there is such psychosis and tension there that is questionable whether it is going to be Vukovar or not." Now at this point, late April 1992, Sarajevo was already being shelled by Bosnian Serb forces; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sarajevo was shelled by regular units and they were attacking the Yugoslav People's Army, irregular unconstitutionally armed units of the two parties, HDZ and SDA. Those are facts that you have in every history textbook. I'm surprised you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, would you refrain from laughing or whatever, and remain silent and listen carefully. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 14712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you're speaking aloud. This is the last warning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue answering the previous question? Or shall I stop here? I have something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it in the hands of Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 2 in the English only. And this is a 2nd Military District report from 8th of April 1992. Towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, under 4th Corps, we read: "During the afternoon, the members of Territorial Defence from Pale municipality opened mortar fire on the sector Vratnik and on the old part of the city of Sarajevo. After the intervention of the command of the 2nd Military District, the fire stopped." Now, this is an example of the urban core of Sarajevo being shelled by Bosnian Serb forces before the conversation we described; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I can explain. You have specific facts about attacks from all infantry weapons on the Yugoslav People's Army precisely at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what we see here in the Yugoslav People's Army's report is that Bosnian Serb forces, to wit, the TO of Pale municipality, are shelling the old part of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you wish to take only that fragment from the whole of that situation, then the answer is yes. I have no reason to doubt what a general of the Yugoslav People's Army says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter 20710 and 14712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P7728 and P7729 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7728 and P7729 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P4583.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, staying with Sarajevo, this is a recording or transcript of the recording of the 50th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, held in Sanski Most in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 354 in the English; 304 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is part of -- one of General Mladic's speeches. And in the middle of the page he says -- in the middle of the page in B/C/S: "When Markale was pounded, you know what happened then" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The top of the page, end of the first paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "But I can say that never in my life was I condemned as I was for Markale." Now on page 61 of your Donia report in English and page 80 in B/C/S, you refer to Dr. Donia quoting this and you write: "This may even have sounded to the author as an admission of guilt by General Mladic that VRS artillery had pounded Markale, causing two instances of large-scale tragedy for the civilians of Sarajevo, but without the missing part of the sentence, it is not possible to see what General Mladic intended to say." Did you bother to check whether any part of the sentence cited by Dr. Donia was actually missing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Could you make it clearer. What you did want to ask? You are asking many questions. Could you put a shorter, clearer question. I would appreciate it. Are you talking about my report? Then tell me the page. You are putting a lot of questions. Please focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I've given the page numbers in both languages in your report. I'm happy to do it again. 61 in the English, 80 in the B/C/S. And to help you understand what I'm put to you at the moment, if we could keep the B/C/S on the screen and call up page 248 in the English of Exhibit P2001, Dr. Donia's highlights report.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. I'm ready. I wanted to assist you to focus. I don't need assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could start with -- you criticised Dr. Donia for leaving out part of the sentence, the missing part of the sentence. Would you first tell us exactly what part of the sentence Mr. Donia left out. That was the simple gist, I think, of the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Certainly. You said it's page 80 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have page 80 in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, the end of that second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no such thing here. I can read to you what's written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... two times the word "Markale" in B/C/S. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I think we are looking at page 80 in Serbian and the Prosecutor meant page 80 in English, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's not correct. There are not even 80 pages in the English version of the report. It's page 80 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, you say, you refer to the quote that Judge Orie directed to you. You say, without the missing part of the sentence a reader can't tell what General Mladic meant. What I'm putting to you is, if you look at the end of the second paragraph on the left side of your screen and you look at footnotes 317 at the bottom on the right side of your screen, what you'll see is there is no missing part of the sentence; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that what I have in front of me does not correspond to that description, I should like to ask you to display this on the screen so I can see it. I'm looking at page 80 in my report and there is no such thing. In order to be able to answer, could I please see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we move on, so we don't have to call up every document repeatedly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could that be the witness has only -- and I have, I think, one side of the screen, left-hand side of the screen is in Cyrillic. Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what I have before me is this document from Sanski Most. It is not my report. I have a printed copy of my report here and there is no such thing on page 80. I can speak on the basis of memory. However, this is a serious court and it makes it incumbent upon me to know exactly what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a Cyrillic text on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have Cyrillic but it's not my report. Do you understand what I'm saying? This is the document from Sanski Most. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... understand what you are saying and the issue now is whether the transcript of the meeting of Sanski Most, what is missing -- what is the missing part which was not quoted by Mr. Donia, that's the first question. Because if you blame him for not giving the full quote, then the first question is: What is missing and you have an opportunity to compare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Uh-huh. [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please tell us what part of the sentence is missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I agree to answer from memory because I still cannot see the section that is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm answering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at this moment comparing the text. You criticised Dr. Donia for -- quotes a text, you say there is a missing part, and we now give the original to you and the simple question is what part was left out by Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that that's what I'm saying. I wish to answer your question but this is my text that is being discussed and the text of Dr. Donia. And the text that was shown to us. Please do show me my text and I will answer your question. Do you understand what I'm saying? There are three documents that are being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we go one step at the time, while we've got this document on the screen, looking at the end of the second paragraph on your left. On your screen, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, that's -- you're looking at the binder --

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... paragraph on the left and the bottom on the right, footnote 317, do you agree that the text is the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, there is a text that is type written. Just tell me which paragraph it is on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: On the left, it's end of the second paragraph, beginning [B/C/S spoken] "kad su tucene Markale." On the right, it's the bottom of the page, footnote 317, beginning [B/C/S spoken] "kad su tucene Markale."

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is all right. That's the footnote. Can I now see what I said. The Prosecutor is asking me about what I wrote. So could you please be so kind as to show me what it is that I wrote, or could you kindly tell me which page this is in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While this is still on the screen, can you confirm that the text is the same or are you unwilling to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course, it's the same. Two sentences are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have D1369 MFI, page 61 in the English and 80 in the B/C/S in e-court. Sorry, the pages have changed from the version we initially received. Can we get page 83 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, yes. And it will be at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you quote Dr. Donia referring to this. You say: "It may have sounded like an admission of guilt." You say: "Without the missing part of the sentence it's not possible to see what General Mladic intended to say." Do we agree now there's no missing part of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer the question, could you please show me in the text itself, Dr. Donia's text. Not the footnote. Could you show me the text itself of Dr. Donia, that page, and then I'm going answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Why are you unable to answer the question now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you not able to show me that page in the report of Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you might prefer to ask the questions, but the reason that you said there was a missing part of the sentence when, in fact, there isn't, is you didn't check this yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can explain as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report of Dr. Donia entitled: Important excerpts from the debate in the Assembly of Republika Srpska, there are many quotations that were taken out of context. We didn't even discuss that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does that mean? That means --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to repeat other generalised criticisms. I'm asking you: You made a criticism here that was wrong because you didn't check the assembly session text yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. It's not fair for the Prosecution to say this. The witness asked whether a further explanation is needed, and he gave a direct answer why he does not accept such a position by the Prosecution explicitly and now he is not allowed to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness should first answer the question and we -- let's go back to the basics. We've seen that Dr. Donia in the footnote quoted a text. You're criticizing him for leaving out a part of the sentence. You've now seen the transcript of the meeting. What part of the sentence is missing? That's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked to see the main body of the text that I used so that I could see that page, and that is what I haven't been able to see until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you have an opportunity to look at that during the next break. If it brings you to further comments, fine; but now you should answer the question. The question is: What part of the sentence is missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this quotation that I provided here and on the basis of what was shown to me here, it doesn't seem that something is missing. However, I say here that this statement made by General Mladic may have sounded like an admission to the author. Taking things out of context can lead us to different conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This ask a specific example of that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're moving away from the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... well. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi. We have now on the record that the witness says that it seems that nothing is missing from that sentence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I repeat the last question of Mr. Traldi. Did you check the -- the transcript of the assembly session yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read what is contained in Dr. Donia's report, and that is contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In -- that means you didn't check the original transcript of the assembly session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was expected to provide an expert opinion on the report of Dr. Donia. I analysed that document. I read the reports from some sessions, and I haven't read reports from other sessions. As a historian, you cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you check this part of the assembly session transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part, no. No. This part, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How were you able to say a part of the speech of Mr. Mladic was missing in the -- in the report of Mr. Donia without checking the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could this page please be shown to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So not the footnote but that page in Dr. Donia's report itself and then I will answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I'm not interested in that anymore. You have answered the question. You didn't check yourself. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Because you didn't read the assembly sessions yourself, you don't know whether particular excerpts accurately reflect the tone of discourse in the assembly, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so when Dr. Donia selects excerpts on the basis of years of comprehensive study of the assembly sessions and you say they might be taken out of context, he is the one who is actually an expert on the context, not you; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the conclusion is that he is making a mistake but I really cannot believe that you are asking me this. Anybody can answer this question for you. No one needs to be a historian to do that. Do allow me to answer. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You've said some things --

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If you'd like to answer the question directly, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Imagine records from the British Parliament. They're called Hansard and they've been published for centuries. And imagine if sections of speeches made by MPs were to be taken out of context --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entirety of their speeches -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is, let's take Hansard as an example. If you had studied those records of the British Parliament for 20 years and you were saying that these are the excerpts that tell you what they were talking about and what their policy was, you'd be doing that on the basis of study, conclusions, expertise. If some guy came along and said, Well, these might be taken out of context without reading the whole transcript, that person's opinion wouldn't be worth very much, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation I received here was "some guy." If that is correct interpretation. I'm a historian and I was asked to come here as an expert. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, try to understand the gist of the question. And don't lose yourself in marginal matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. These are marginal matters. So your position is that from the outset we should appreciate the knowledge and experience of Dr. Donia. That cannot be the position of an impartial observer. He could have studied something for 20 years and reached erroneous conclusions. His report shows that he is partial and that he is avoiding sources, and that's my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. The quote which is found in your report ends with three dots after the word "Markale." I see that it's both true for the B/C/S version and for the English version. Were you under the impression when you wrote this down that something else was following?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you then check whether that was true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I kindly asked to have a look at the main text, so I could see what it says there, and persistently the text is not being shown to me. You understand? I need to see what it was that I looked at, when I looked at the main body of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have an opportunity to -- I take it that the relevant page can be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll arrange for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will get that during the break and you can look at it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now what General Mladic had said next was: "Mr. President, I've never, because I'm a professional soldier, I respect my profession because of the people who have to follow it. I have never turned off the gas in Sarajevo nor was the gas turned off on my orders without you knowing it." Now that's an admission that Mladic ordered the gas turned off in Sarajevo. He's just saying Karadzic knew too; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He says here, "I never turned off." "Never turned off." That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "Without you knowing it." That means: When I did it, you knew about it. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you cannot interpret it that way, this sentence. We cannot know what the author of the sentence wanted to say. You have to ask him. I'm not a psychoanalyst. I'm a historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So now you don't know what the right interpretation is; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood your question, but the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have P431, page 38 in English and 32 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This will be General Mladic's speech at the 16th Assembly. He says at the bottom of the page in English: "We should not say we will destroy Sarajevo. We need Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where is it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe it's at the top, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "We are not going to say that we are going to destroy the power supply pylons or turn off the water supply. No. Because that would get America out of its seat. But, gentlemen, please, fine, well, one day there is no water at all" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have not found the place. Could we please have a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please locate exactly from where you are reading and perhaps repeat the reading, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Approximately the tenth line from the bottom in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Does that suffice for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Working on it. Found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll start from the beginning. "We should not say we will destroy Sarajevo. We need Sarajevo. We are not going to say that we are going to destroy the power supply pylons or turn off the water supply. No. Because that would get America out of its seat. But, gentlemen, please, fine, well, one day there is no water at all in Sarajevo, what is it we do not know, damage, we should fix it, no, we will fix it, slowly. And the same with the electrical power." So what General Mladic is declaring, the day he was appointed commander is the intents to manipulate the supply of basic humanitarian needs to the population of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you are doing the same thing that Mr. Donia did in his report --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this report of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- is one question at a time and I'd ask you to answer those questions. Are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course. I don't know if you're able to put one single question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I read you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, now you stop commenting on whether Mr. Traldi puts the right question or not. Mr. Stojanovic is in a position to object to any question which is unclear or not. It's not for you. If you don't understand the question, you can say, I don't understand the question. But here you're simply invited to tell us why you think that this text is not about the manipulation of the basic supplies, as Mr. Traldi put it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because already in the next sentence that Mr. Traldi has omitted, there is a reference to electricity and water being turned off for the JNA. It's the very next sentence. Same method. Just like Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah. The next sentence Donia -- the next sentence Mladic says, "Zadar and Sibenik and Split, they disconnected the army's power supply. The army had none for six months, but I told them while I'm here, you will not get it and they didn't, apart from when I felt like letting them have some." So as you do with Dr. Donia's reports what you've just done is grasp for a different explanation but, in fact, the JNA barracks that you were referring to, one, were in Croatia, and, two, were used by General Mladic as he brags about here as a pretext for cutting off utilities to cities in Croatia. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, that was in Yugoslavia, not Croatia. At the time Yugoslavia existed as an internationally recognised state and they are attacking the regular army, the JNA. I cannot believe you're putting this question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, you apparently are mixing up two things. First, what Mr. Mladic said he would do, which is understood by Mr. Traldi as manipulating the supply of basic needs; second - and that's a totally different question - whether in history or on the basis of what happened elsewhere that there may have been good reasons for doing that or it can be explained why one would wish to do that. But we are now focussing now, first of all, on the first question, that is, what Mr. Mladic said, whether that is an example of manipulating the supply of basic needs. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat: I'm a historian, I'm not a psychologist. Manipulation, non-manipulation, you have to ask the person who said that. If you want me to confirm that what is written here is written her, I can confirm that. But you don't need a historian for that, you can get anybody who can read Cyrillic, regardless of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is context that a historian is supposed to deal with. Yes, that is what is written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For context you first have to know context is given for what and that is what Mr. Traldi asked you about. Let's move on. If you continue to avoid the questions and to rather refer to the background where the questions are about the core of what is written, this may devaluate your evidence and you should be aware of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Two sentences later, Mladic says: "Therefore, we have to wisely tell the world it was they who were shooting, hit the transmission line and the power went off. They were shooting at the water supply facilities. There was a power" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- "cut at such and such a place, we are doing our best repairing it. This is what diplomacy is." Now, one of the bits of context that would be interesting for a statement like this from a commander is orders from his immediate subordinates to carry out of the same policy; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could be the context. But the context of this statement is also the attack against Serbs and against the JNA or, rather, at this moment, the Army of Republika Srpska. That is the primary context. The war had started. The endangerment of the Serb areas of Sarajevo. And, of course, firing at the JNA or, rather, the Army of Republika Srpska. That's the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter - and I'll be very quick with this document, Your Honour - 06129. I was perhaps a little quick. 06129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, low volume. Mr. Mladic, low volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see a Drina Corps order from the 31st of May, 1993. The deputy commander Colonel Skocajic is relaying a verbal order from the corps commander, Colonel Zivanovic, to demolish the water tower and tank in the area of Zeleni Jadar, the water supply system for Srebrenica. He writes: "Since this has not been done so far, this task is to be executed immediately, by June 1, 1993 at the latest, and it is to be presented to the public as if Muslim forces did it." Now that's the same policy we saw Mladic saying and calling diplomacy, destroying the water supply in the surrounded area and presenting it as if the Muslims had done it to themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There, you have the statement of General Mladic in the assembly. Here, you have an order by a colonel who gave a verbal order to a lieutenant-colonel and -- Lieutenant-Colonel Urosevic. You said you would show us this order. You showed us a verbal order of a colonel to the lieutenant-colonel. It's unbelievable how you connect these things, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 06129 that will be Exhibit P7730, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'm really puzzled by your last answer, Witness. Are you saying that what was said in that assembly session, that is, doing A, saying that someone else did it or that you didn't do it, is not similar to what we find here in a still military context, doing A, saying that someone else did it. That is, just lying about what you did. Do you see that there's some corresponding elements in what was said in the assembly meeting and here, as far as the content, the gist of it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a similarity, there are corresponding elements, et cetera. This is not proof. I did not say that this was a corresponding element or a similarity. I said, in principle, people -- things can be similar. But this is not evidence. It's not an order by General Mladic. You have his words in the assembly, and you have one colonel and one lieutenant-colonel. No, this is no proof. No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't bother about what is evidence of what, because you are here just to answer the questions. And whether it's evidence or not, I think you should leave that, after we've heard the parties on it, to us. We take a break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could the witness be provided with the relevant portion of Dr. Donia's report. And if you would have the number for us again so that we can look at it on our screens as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's P2001. And the reason I called up the footnote in the English is the B/C/S is across two pages which I'll track down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll be able to follow if there's any comment from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's highlight 317 in both versions, for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, a footnote always refers to the main text, and that's what the witness may want to have a look at. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I put shortly on the record the following. It's an issue pertaining -- pertinent to the testimony of Savo Strbac. In the interests of transparency, the Chamber informs the parties that an article authored by witness Savo Strbac, entitled, "How I testified for Mladic" has come to the Chamber's attention. This article was published in print and online by the Serbian news outlet Vecernje Novosti on 19 November, 2015. The Chamber leaves it to the parties as to whether there should be any follow-up on the point. But if we became aware of it then I think it would be appropriate for you to know that we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32544.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may say something. Keep it brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've looked at what has been given me, and I can tell you my opinion. I absolutely stand by what I wrote in my report concerning that statement of General Mladic in the assembly. I've read the relevant part. I stand by what I've written, and thank you very much for showing it to me. It's only appropriate to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a bit confused. Because earlier you said there was no missing part of the sentence and in your report you say a part of the sentence is missing. Now, to what extent do you still say there's a part missing, of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to explain. It's about the three dots that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... three dots, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. I have before me, Page 184 of the report by Dr. Donia. That's the page in his text in B/C/S, or in Serbian. It's 135, page 135 there is a footnote. I don't think you have the opportunity to see it now but it would be good for you to look at it. What it looks like in the report by Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we have access on our computers to the report at this moment. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hm. So once again, page 184 in B/C/S, 135 in English, the footnote. What is this about, in fact? Look at how Dr. Donia quoted the statement by Mladic. It runs counter to the basic rules of the profession of historian. If you are able to look at it now, please look at it. It's fragment 317. It says: "When Markale was targeted, you know all what happened, but I was never in my life criticized like then." And then three dots. Those are the three dots you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see your point. You repeated that, and you concluded from the fact that there were, as a matter of fact, in the original report four dots - not three but that's a detail - that you thought if he quotes it this way, there must be something else. He left that out. And without checking, you just concluded that what was left out, which finally is not left out, that you concluded that that missing part would shed a different light on what he said. Is that -- that you are blaming Dr. Donia for adding the dots and that you fully, professionally, dealt with that by not checking the original source and concluding that what was missing, which is not missing, would have changed the meaning of it? I have no other way of understanding if you draw our attention to the dots. Please -- when I'm wrong, please briefly explain why I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every profession has its own clear rules. When you are citing a source, if you put three dots - there are three dots here, and I'm speaking about the B/C/S version - that means you left something out. These are rules of the profession. Each profession has its own strict rules. They were not observed here. And just very briefly, a reader who reads this -- and you will notice in the English version which I also have before me, the next paragraph begins with quotation marks - that's the English version - and when the next paragraph happens, that means that something is really missing. So what is the conclusion? A reader reading this in this case, me -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me stop you there. It's very clear that quoting something with dots where nothing follows, you pointed out that that's against the rules of your profession. Now, my next question would be is it within the rules of your profession without knowing what was left out, without even checking the original source that to criticise that the meaning would you quite different with the left-out part, is that within the rules of your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, and I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think that you explained that you didn't check the original source and you say that's within the rules of your profession. That's fine. Let's move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was not my explanation. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 29 May 1992 "New York Times" article entitled; Serbian gunners pound Sarajevo. It begins by stating: "Defying international threats of sanctions against Belgrade, Serbian forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina pounded Sarajevo with artillery and rocket fire early today in the heaviest bombardment the capital of the war-torn republic has faced, and kept up the shelling throughout the day, officials and witnesses there said." Now, you mentioned the shelling on Vase Miskina Street on the 27th of May in your report but you do not mention this shelling; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donia meticulously noted down all the shellings. There was no need for me to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, the article is from the 29th of May, published on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have 65 ter 33103.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a Bosnian MUP investigative file for shelling on 28 May 1992 at 2355 hours at Dzemala Bijedica Street, number 78. We see from the table of contents it includes the death certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 3 in both versions. This is Official Note from the file. The note states in pertinent part in the second paragraph: "On 28 May 1992, at 2355 hours, Gacanin, Edina has noticed a huge lightning coming from the direction of Lukavica towards her window, after which a tremendous blow was heard at the corner of the wall between the kitchen and dining-room, following the tremendous detonation in the corridor as a consequence of which a big hole was created, through which Edina fell down into the apartment underneath." And it said -- it says at the end she learned later that her neighbour, Simo Sigud, 74 years old, died. Now I have two questions. First, Lukavica was held by the VRS in May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And second, this is an example of the indiscriminate shelling of civilian areas in Sarajevo that caused the suffering that you referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is completely irrelevant to the subject of my expertise, and I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33102.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a 26 February 1995 Bosnian MUP Novo Sarajevo report on activity in the area of Velesici since the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 in the B/C/S; 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the middle of the page in the B/C/S, we see an entry for the 28th of May, 1992. We see: "Between 2200 and 0600 hours the Velesici area was shelled from the aggressor's positions at Mrkovici, at which time there was significant material damage to facilities and Salko Fatkic suffered minor injures." Mrkovici was also held by the VRS in May of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And this is an another irrelevant document from Muslim sources. I'm not sure that you have read my report, actually, Mr. Traldi, because if you had read it, my main objection is systematic use of sources from only one side. I still am waiting for you to show a document about the suffering of Serb people, rapes of women committed by people like Caco, Dedo, Celo. I expect that from you, Mr. Traldi, in the interests of truth and justice. I'm not sure you read my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I tender the last three documents, 32544, 33103, and 33102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 32544 will be Exhibit P7731. 65 ter number 33103 will be Exhibit P7732. And 33102 will be Exhibit P7733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7731 to P7733 are all three admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 03815.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, turning to the Serb-claimed areas of Sarajevo, you know there were massive Muslim departures from those areas during 1992 and 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just as Muslims kept Serbs in their part of Sarajevo by force, held them in private prisons and killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, so this is a report from the Rajlovac Red Cross, 1993. We see it's filled out for Rajlovac. Now, Rajlovac was one of the municipalities the Serbs had established in the Sarajevo area; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And before the war, it was part of Novi Grad municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we see the latest information the Red Cross is reporting is about 5.000 people live in Rajlovac, of which 98 per cent are Serbs. This is an example of the massive departures of Muslims that we just talked about; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Just as Sarajevo, as a city, as a whole, was left by 157.000 Serbs after its so-called liberation. I am waiting for you to mention that too. 157.000 Serbs. Thousands of Yugoslavs disappeared from Sarajevo. Where are they, Mr. Traldi? Maybe Ghostbusters chased them out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovic, stop giving this kind of comment. Answer the questions. And I have one question for you before we continue. If others - and that may well have happened and I'm serious about that - if others committed crimes, does that make crimes by another party any less a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a good question. I am not contesting the crimes that were committed by Serbs. Really not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please refrain from -- we are not writing the history of the whole of the war. We are called to have a trial in which no doubt about that, where responsibility for an accused has to be established or not. You are insisting again and again and again on that others committed crimes as well. Not to say whether they did or they did not, but that's perhaps as background sometimes of some importance but that's not the core of this case. I want you to understand it, that we're not writing history of war but that we are preparing a judgement, whatever that judgement will be, on an indictment against one accused. Would you please keep that in mind because that also shows there's no need to again and again and again to draw the attention to the crimes committed by others which may well be the case. I'm not in any way expressing myself or the Chamber is not expressing itself on that. But there's no need at this moment. And also you do not have to invite Mr. Traldi to bring any opinion about what others did. You apparently have difficulties in understanding what a criminal trial is, so you are hereby urged to refrain from such comments. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you mention in your Donia report the VRS quickly achieved the capture of [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... listen to the next question of Mr. Traldi and answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mention in your Donia report that the VRS quickly achieved the capture of key military and industrial complexes in areas including Rajlovac, we agree that you did not mention that when the VRS took over Rajlovac non-Serbs, large numbers of non-Serbs were expelled; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a irrelevant question. It was not the subject of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is an irrelevant question or not is not for you to decide. Please answer the question. If you can. If you can't, please tell us you can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a historian, and you are saying I should not be speaking about history. You invited me as a historian, as an expert. This question can be answered by someone who is not a historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the Defence has called you as an expert witness. Listen to the next question of Mr. Traldi and answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can answer the previous question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said I can refuse to answer a question, Your Honour. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I say that if you can't answer a question [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... right. I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Previous translation continues] ... the only reason why you can't answer a question is because you do not know the answer. If that is what you are telling us, please make that clear. Is it that you can't answer it because you have no knowledge, direct or indirect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot contest that parts of the city of Sarajevo controlled by the Serbs were left by a certain amount of population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those people were expelled; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 22933.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this shows -- this is a decision on the appointment of the municipal commission for the 1993 census in Vogosca. You're aware the Republika Srpska did a census in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 22935.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this is a table that was put together in the Karadzic case on the basis of 65 ter 02559, the 1991 census, and 65 ter 22934, the 1993 Vogosca census results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And for the Defence the relevant part of 65 ter 02559 is pages 44 through 47 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at just a couple of entries here on the first page, we see second, D. Vogosca, 1991, 124 Muslims; 1993, just a line. No representation of any Muslims. Kremis, 1991, 59; 1993, none. Krivoglavci, 1991, 61; 1993, zero. Semizovac, we see, turning to page 2 in the English, 1991, 427; 1993, 16. And there are other examples, Svrake 1991, 1036; 1993, zero. This is another example of the large-scale flight by Muslims from the Serb-claimed areas of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is evidence that there is no Muslim population in these places anymore. This is not evidence of ethnic cleansing. These are numbers, tables, showing that these people are no longer there. And one more thing. If I may, you said Blagovac in 1991, there were 16 Muslims and I think you said something else, 160 or something. 16, in fact, and then in 1993, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you introduced yourself the ethnic cleansing. That was not part of the question. That was flight of Muslims and apparently you are defending or you are responding to matters which are not put to you in the question. Would you carefully listen to the question and the way in which Mr. Traldi phrases it and then answer that question rather than a question you may have on your mind but which was not put to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender the last three documents: 65 ter 03815, 22933, and 22935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 03814 will be Exhibit P7734. 22933 will be Exhibit P7735. And 22935 will be Exhibit P7736.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7734 through P7736 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 06017.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, sir, you know one of the ways that Muslims were removed from the Serb-claimed municipalities around Sarajevo was through exchanges; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were exchanges. Of course, I do not accept your interpretation, but, yes, there were exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, the results of the exchanges was Muslims who had previously lived in the Serb-claimed areas now lived in the urban core of Sarajevo; right? One of the results of the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this is a letter from the Bosnian exchange commission chair Filip Vuckovic. He mentions a proposal for discussion on further exchanges. He says several have been carried out. It refers to the Vrbanija bridge, Brijesca, Ilidza. I'm just waiting for the transcript, sir. Those are all places in the Sarajevo area; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now turning to page 5 in the English, and I'm afraid we don't have the full document in the B/C/S so I'll come back to it. Can we have 65 ter 20851. Now this is an intercepted conversation between Momcilo Mandic and Momcilo Krajisnik dated 26th June 1992. Turning to page 3 in both languages, Mandic says, "There this Vuckovic, a member of the youth organisation, a Serb, who is criticizing us because we have 400 prisoners here, you know?" And Krajisnik asks if he's a Communist and what he wants. And Mandic says: "He is the president of that exchange commission." Krajisnik asks: "Their commission?" Mandic says: "Yes." And Krajisnik asks: "And what is it that he wants?" And Mandic says: "War prisoners, no, they are ex for them. They're hardly interested in people, they are interested in ammunition and meat and now we let those women and children go to Vrbanija, to go to their own people, he says that's ethnic cleansing what we do ..." That's a reflection of Vrbanija, one of the locations we saw in Vuckovic's letter being a place that women and children were exchanged in the urban core of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to explain something here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may explain, but only explain what is an answer to the question. Don't explain things which are not included in the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source that is being used here is an intercepted telephone conversation. As a historian, I have to ask about the source. This is typed up. From the point of view of history as a science, this document is not relevant and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, please answer the question. This Chamber will deal with any authenticity matter that is relevant for us. Please answer the question. And if you say you can't answer that, then -- because you have no knowledge of it, but don't be bothered about authenticity. Because that's for the parties to raise and for the Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were exchanges of civilians, and there were opinions amongst the Serbs that the Presidency and Alija Izetbegovic do not really care very much about the lives of their civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm what we read out just now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about civilians. Women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that. There were exchanges of civilians. I cannot confirm that. Civilians were exchanged. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 20851. Ms. Stewart has the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P7737, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We saw a reference to prisoners. You know but don't mention in your report that large numbers of non-Serb civilians were held prisoner in the Serb-claimed areas around Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is irrelevant for my report. There were prisoners on both sides, yes, including prisoners that were held by Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Including large numbers of non-Serb civilians in those areas; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There's no reason to contest that. The number? Well, the number hasn't been ascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 15189.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a 21 December 1992 SRK command telegram order to Butmir KP Dom. That's one of the places that those civilians were detained; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I mean, I see the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now it says: "Pursuant to the order you ought to seek the correspond commander's approval prior to every exchange of prisoners of war." If we could have -- sorry, just very briefly we see it refers to an order of the Republika Srpska minister of justice. If we could have 65 ter 12812. It gives the number 1/2-243. Here we see an order, number 1/2-243 from the minister of justice of Republika Srpska, to all penal and correctional institutions. An order instructing the personnel of the main facilities of penal and correctional institutions housing and guarding prisoners of war not to carry out exchanges without the prior approval of the president of a competent high court and the commands of the corps in charge. Did you consider it relevant for your report that the VRS had control of the Muslims who were detained in the Sarajevo area, that they couldn't be exchanged without the corps commander's approval?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Robert Donia writes about all of that. There was no need for me to go back to these topics. That was covered in his report. You have the report of your expert historian that you retained. Why would I write about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I take it you don't dispute any of that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm able to read the text that is in front of me. That's the way it was written. That is what is written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that wasn't the question. The question is whether you dispute that the VRS had control over the Muslims who were detained, they couldn't be exchanged without the corps commander's approval. That was the question, whether you contest that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can accept that, yes. Yes, there's no reason -- yes, there's no reason for me to contest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 03797.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a list from the VRS commission for exchange and release labelled Kula prison list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we turn to the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see Captain Bulajic's name, the head of the commission for exchange, and in the bottom right, the commander of the SRK, General Galic. Does that refresh your recollection as to whether Kula was one of the places that the Muslims were detained in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several places where civilians were detained on the Serb and on the Muslim side. In Muslim prisons there weren't any lists of this kind. This shows that there was some organisation here as opposed to the private prisons that the Muslims had. So I can confirm what I see before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender, first, the Vuckovic letter for which we've now fixed the upload that was referred to in the intercepted conversation, that's 65 ter 06017, and then this series of the last three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that letter the one where you said we don't have the complete document and therefore we'll move on. Did you intend to put any question to the witness in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The link I was going to draw was the link between the location mentioned, the Vrbanija bridge in the letter and the location referred to as well as the author, Mr. Vuckovic, who is then referred to in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you don't need the witness for that. That's your ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] put to him that it's the same person and the same location, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 06017 will be Exhibit P7738. 65 ter number 15189 will be Exhibit P7739. 65 ter 12812 will be Exhibit P7740. And 65 ter 03797 will be Exhibit P7741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections raised by the Defence, P7738 through P7741 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to a different topic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 07871. I'm sure it was my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a diary of the ICFY negotiating team from April and the beginning of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 46 in the English, 82 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This reflects a meeting on the 24th of April, beginning at 9.00 a.m. with the Bosnian Serbs. Refers to Karadzic, Mladic, Krajisnik. Turning to page 48 in the English, 86 in the B/C/S. And if I could just have a second. We don't have ... the B/C/S of the part that I was interested in. We do now. We see that the author - the Chamber has received evidence that that's one of the negotiators named Herbert Okun records, "RM wants entire west bank of Drina." I asked you this morning if Bijeljina and Zvornik were Serb claimed areas, and you said, well, there were strategic objectives but some territories could be exchanged. The truth is Mladic's position was the entire west side of the Drina had to be Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the position of General Mladic, necessarily. I can read his statements here for you. Just as you read General Mladic's statements, I have some statements here too, those that are contained in Dr. Donia's reports, and they testified to something completely different. These are parts of his speeches from the assembly not this kind of source. I can read it out for you, I can tell you about it. I can tell you that General Mladic says, Let us not go to places that are not our own. We are just going to defend our own homes. This is a defensive war. As for towns themselves, I already said that within those six strategic objectives that you mentioned yesterday it is quite clear that borders were not clearly marked. They were open and that they would be the result precisely of such talks as those referred to here. As for this source that you showed here, if I'm not mistaken, this is an American negotiator. A moment ago on this that you showed us, it was obvious that Vance and Owen were under enormous pressure from the U.S.A. to give the Muslims as much as possible, so I have to say that this source is a very highly contested one as far as I'm concerned. This is an American negotiator. You will correct me if I am wrong. This is, indeed, an interested party, so allow me to challenge the objectivity. As for General Mladic's statements, they are contained in the report of Dr. Treanor, these are important speeches and I can show you this and can you have it there so General Mladic says, No, we're just going to defend what is ours. Even the Army of China could not attain the objectives that you have set out here. So what you quoted yesterday, the statement of General Mladic from his interview that is one thing.
