By the way it is not called Nin as you called it. It is called Nin. One should know a bit of Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that this document be marked for identification. We'll separate out this meeting and ask that this meeting be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please reserve a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the number reserved will be Exhibit P7742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is reserved for an excerpt still to be uploaded. Witness, is there any specific reason why you contest the accuracy of what Mr. Okun did write down on this page, apart from that you don't trust him as a -- as a part of a negotiating team which had its own interests? But do you have any reason to say, Well, this is -- he wrote this down for himself but he wrote down something which was not said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to respond to you as a historian. That's how I was brought here. These are his notes. And the United States is a highly interested party in this war. They even became a warring party once they went to war. That's what it's all it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you told already and then I asked you a different question. Do you have any reason why, in this notebook, which are -- is supposed to serve the memory of Mr. Okun, why he would have written down here something what was not said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, that's one of the rules of the craft. Just likes Zimmermann's notes. I can believe it but not necessarily. I can say, yes, I agree, but I have to keep a certain distance. Do you understand that? It is one of the rules of the craft. Each and every profession and job has rules of its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it's not an answer to my question, it's clear that you do not have any specific reason why it would be not be accurate what he wrote down here. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02368. That will be page 42 in the English and 43 in the B/C/S, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this is part of the transcript of the 23rd Session of the RS Assembly dated the 19th of January, 1993. Did you ever look at that session in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was to read Robert Donia's report and I carried out my task very conscientiously and very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to the question. If you continue to refuse answer questions, we have to consider what to do with that. The question simply was whether you consulted this transcript of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I did not. Just show me the date then and let's see where and when it was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So on the one hand you say, no, I didn't consult it. At the same time you do not know what date it is. Mr. Traldi, what date is it. We could go, perhaps, to the relevant page and then we put the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi already explained it to you: 19th of January, 1993. You should have listened to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have not seen the transcript. No, I haven't. I saw what I found in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is part of the remarks by Rajko Djukic. Do you know what his position was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has evidence that he was the SDS co-ordinator for the Birac region and president of their executive committee. He says in the second paragraph: "It is clear to everyone that there can no be Serbian state nor a community of Serbian states nor life or prospects for the Serbian people without Podrinje from Foca to Bijeljina." This is an example of, again, the whole Drina area being claimed by the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You quoted the statement of a gentleman who came from a small part of Republika Srpska who was in charge of that particular part. He does not represent that group that makes key decisions. This is just one statement made in the assembly. You have to make a distinction between decision-makers and those who are at a far lower level. That's a basic rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the president -- and perhaps I was ambiguous when I set out his position, the president of the SDS executive committee for all of Bosnia. That's not just somebody from a small part responsible for that part; right? That's one of the national leaders.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is in question, then the relevance of the statement goes up. A moment ago you said that he was co-ordinator for Birac and president of the Executive Council for Birac. That's what you said a moment ago. And now you've changed what you said. Let us just establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P355, page 60 in English and 68 in B/C/S. And as it comes up, I'd ask that that session be marked and we'll excerpt Mr. Djukic's reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you already reserve a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number reserved for 65 ter 02368 will be P7743.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, reserved for excerpts of the minutes to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could have page 60 in both languages. We have the transcript in B/C/S but that will be, I think, easier to work with anyway? And we see here an entry in General Mladic' notebook from 17 September 1992, a meeting with the Foca Tactical Group, we see at the start a reference to its commander, Colonel Kovac. And turning to page 66 in both languages, we see Mladic's remarks over Miroslav Stanic, the head of the War Presidency: "Foca was supposed to be the second Islamic centre for Muslims in Europe. The population of Foca before the war was 42.000, of which number around 51 per cent were Muslims, 49 per cent Serbs and Montenegrins. Now the percentage of Serbs in Foca is 99 per cent." Now, this is an example of the combination of the first goal, ethnic separation, with the third goal, Serb control of the Drina valley, as Mladic and Djukic said in the last two exhibits we saw; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The first objective was separation. It doesn't say expulsion anywhere. The third is control over Eastern Bosnia. It's not written there anywhere that anyone should be expulsed. So my answer is emphatically no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P431.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any -- In your question, Mr. Traldi, at least in the English, it's transcribed as the first goal ethnic separation, whereas the witness in his answer said the first objective was separation, it doesn't say expulsion anywhere, so I do not know whether the witness heard your words be translated as "expulsion" or whether it was translated to him in B/C/S as "separation." Witness, did you hear that in your own language that the word "expulsion" was used or was it translated to you as "separation"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we read here in court the six strategic objectives. We've read the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to know is whether the words of Mr. Traldi where he said "ethnic separation," whether that was translated to you as "separation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I cannot testify what was said. I can only testify how I understood his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your answer was absolutely not. The first objective was separation. It doesn't say expulsion anywhere, which suggests that the question by Mr. Traldi was translated to you in terms of expulsion. If that's the case, then I will invite Mr. Traldi to repeat the question. If it is not the case, then we do not understand your answer criticising that another word was used; whereas, Mr. Traldi, at least in English, used the word "separation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer. Just exactly as it is written here. You have a correct translation into English of what Mr. Traldi said. He was talking about the six objectives, strategic objectives. Ethnic separation combined in his question with the third objective, the valley of the river Drina. I understood it implies the expulsion of people. This is about expulsion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so I do understand now that it was translated to you in your own language as "separation" but you interpreted that as including expulsion and, therefore, you answered the question not on the basis of what Mr. Traldi asked you but on the basis of your own interpretation of his words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if that's not the case, then I have to establish that you didn't answer my previous question. Let move on. We'll consider whether or not to verify how it was explained to you in your own language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock. And I see we're at the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're at the time for a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I use the time to briefly deal with a matter which is the filing of Rule 92 bis attestations. On 9 November of this year, the Defence filed Rule 92 bis attestations for Zeljka Malinovic and Dragan Malinovic which have been uploaded into e-court with the relevant statements attached. The Defence requests that the statements that were conditionally admitted into evidence be replaced by the new versions. The Chamber hereby grants the Defence's request, instructs the Registry to replace D1231 and D1235 with the newly uploaded versions and confirms the admission of D1231 with associated exhibits D1232 to D1234 and D1235 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we please have P6730. And it's MNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a document coming from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina's state exchange commission. It's dated 10 February, 1993. It refers in the first paragraph to girls of Muslim ethnicity being held captive and abused in a brothel in Miljevina. That's in Foca, the municipality we were just discussing; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 5 in the English, 4 in the B/C/S, we see Izetbegovic issue a decision pardoning convicted person named Nikola Ostojic. And page 6 in the English, 5 in the B/C/S, the second exchange referenced that Ostojic is exchanged for five people, including at least three women. So the exchanges of women also happened in the area covered by the third strategic objective in the Drina area; right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, with the proviso that -- never mind, I'll stick with yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we saw in General Mladic's notebook that Foca had become 99 per cent Serb. Holding people in what is referred to as a brothel until they are exchanged is the sort of thing that would drive people out of the region as soon as they had an opportunity to go; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, just as in brothels for Serbian women held by Muslim soldier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I asked that that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same number but not any further marked not admitted but now admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to clear up. It has its P number. Does it mean the whole document is coming in or will it receive a new number? What is the proposal of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm tendering the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar, the number already assigned was ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6730, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the status changed from marked not admitted to admitted into evidence. Witness, I notice that you persistently continue to always refer, if the question is about what happens in brothels, you are immediately, although not asked, referring to brothels held by other parties. You were invited not to do that. And I urge you again to not do that. Because it's not part of the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33348.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a list for exchange. We see the receipt stamp from the Bosnian Ministry of Defence, Tuzla District Secretariat, that it comes from the Serbian armed forces command of the Chetnik assault detachment, commission for exchange of prisoners of war in Pelemisi. We can turn to page 3 in both languages, please. We see a list of what are referred to as: "Your people for exchange." Just taking a quick look, we see Muslim names here; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if you look at, for instance, numbers 17, 18, 19, 30, 31, and 38, you see their ages, they're all minors; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not seen in the Serbian text or perhaps the copy is bad, but I see it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, if you look at number 17, you see a handwritten "16 G" next to it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can vaguely see it, but then very next passage is totally invisible but I see it in English translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And G is the first letter of the word "godine" or year in Bosnian and Serbian languages; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The fact that these names are accompanied by numbers somebody is obviously taking into account and taking care to mention that they are minors. They're not treated like all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, for numbers 17, 18, 19, which have the minor notes, we see Meriz Nevladin [phoen] and Kadir Manjic, and at number 38, if we scroll to the right in B/C/S and a little bit up we see Ferida Osmanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The English -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to remember those names for a moment and ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I just ask one question. If you look at numbers, and perhaps we move to the left again, numbers -- could we scroll a bit down. Numbers 29, 30, and 31. By the names, could you in any way tell us whether that gives a clue to the gender of these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these are girls. These are women's names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question. With respect to the minors, you said they are not treated like all the rest. How do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I see what is shown to me, and I see that only next to some names age is indicated, which implies that somebody is paying attention to the fact that they are minors. You see that other names have no age indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you don't know that they are treated like all the rest. They are only referred to in a different way in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said. I said I supposed that somebody was taking care of this, since they've written it down. I -- that's all I can say, based on what I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd tender 65 ter 33348, which was the list for exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7745, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 06009.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the transcript. I have the same on both screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you now have a B/C/S version on your screen? The transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not my question. I have documents on both screens. I don't see the LiveNote anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and could -- could the usher assist and see whether ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will reappear very soon. It's a consequence of moving from private session into open session so it will be there in a second. The more we talk, the sooner it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, this is the 21 January 1993 session of the council for co-ordinating state policy. If we turn to page 59 in the English, 70 in the B/C/S, and if we can turn one page back in the B/C/S, just to get the start. And we see Mr. Karadzic is speaking and he refers to exchange. And then in the second paragraph, he says: "We now have to make" -- and we're turning to the next page in the B/C/S at the top. Second sentence: "We now have to make arrests again, so as to be able to" -- Turning to the next page in English: "... exchange." So what he is stating is a policy of indiscriminately arresting non-Serbs for exchange; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the next sentence: "They are keeping Serbs in the village. They are asking for seven criminals in exchange for civilians." You are again taking a sentence out of context. So my answer is no, and I explained why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand you would like to focus on what they, which I take to be the other side is doing. What Karadzic is saying is, We have to arrest people, not because they've committed any crime, but so we can exchange them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is written here. That's what I received. That's only I can say. But that's all I can say about this document, together with the sentence that follows, which says that Muslims are keeping Serbian civilians and they want seven criminals in exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 20 in the English, 22 in the B/C/S. At the bottom we see Karadzic is speaking and he says, starting in the second sentence: "There was 50/50 of us in Zvornik. The number of inhabitants of Zvornik is now the same, approximately 50.000 and they are all Serbs. More than 24.000 Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia have arrived and stopped in Zvornik" --

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, it's not visible here. I have the impression that this is the wrong page. I can't see that statement by Radovan Karadzic. It's in English here, but it's not here in Serbian. Could we just see the next page in Serbian? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think we do now have page 22 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what Karadzic says is: "There was 50/50 of us in Zvornik. The number of inhabitants of Zvornik is now the same, approximately 50.000, and they are all Serbs. More than 24.000 Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia have now arrived and stopped in Zvornik." Now, first, I asked about Zvornik and Bijeljina and whether they were claimed by the Bosnian Serbs this morning, does the fact, as Karadzic says, that Zvornik had become entirely Serb-populated refresh your recollection as to whether it was claimed by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs took over Zvornik. From the Muslim perspective, they captured it. From the Serbian perspective, it was liberated. But I stand by my position. It is not part of the six strategic objectives discussed yesterday. You can see from this that Serbs had been expelled from Zvornik. That's what you've just read. From Tuzla, they were violently, mercilessly expelled. That's what you've just read, from Zenica, from Central Bosnia, and I would add Tuzla as a special example of the ethnic cleansing of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Where's Zvornik relative to the Drina river?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I go at least twice a month to Zvornik. I know that place very well. It's just as if I asked you where New York is relative to the Hudson river. You want me to answer? It's on the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you could have left out the whole explanation because we do not travel with you twice a month. So if you would have just said it's at the Drina river then would you have answered the question. It seems that it amuses you. It doesn't amuse the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the third witness this meeting has been used with. I think we have used five or six different portions. We can meet with the Defence, but under those circumstances, I would think it would be reasonable exceptionally to have the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic. 79 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I grant that it's an exception, Your Honours, but it's been used several times in many different parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it helps for the whole document to be admitted, we don't object. But it should be one document under one P number; I think that would be practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole of the document will be marked for identification. The Chamber will consider whether or not, because I don't have the clear recollection of what portions were used or not, but whether that justifies the admission of all 79 pages, we'll have a look at that. For the time being, the whole of the document would, Mr. Registrar, receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P7746, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02382. I don't believe we have the right document. 02382. And it should be the 34th Session of the RS Assembly which doesn't look like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, may I leave the courtroom for a moment? Is that allowed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the usher will accompany you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can use the time meanwhile for other matters. First the remaining issue from the testimony of Savo Strbac. Exhibit P7646. On the 12th of November of this year, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence, first, advising that the redacted B/C/S version of Exhibit P7646 had been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter number 33419a, and, second, requesting that the corrected version, now consistent with the English version, replace what is currently contained in Exhibit P7646. The Chamber instructs the Registry to replace Exhibit P7646 with the document uploaded under 65 ter number 34419a. Mr. Stojanovic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Just one request while this brief pause is on, could Mr. Mladic leave the courtroom. He needs to go to the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not oppose, although we would continue in the meantime unless you would say, let's take an early break but then the last session would be a little bit over one hour. So it's up to you whether we take an early break and then Mr. Mladic being present all the time or that -- or that he would agree that we'll continue while he is leaving the courtroom. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just have a second?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, can we have an early break and a longer session after that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take an early break. And we will -- first of all, the witness -- we'd like to see you back, Mr. Kovic, in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just so it doesn't get lost we don't need the witness but the transcript, I believe, recorded 65 ter 334419a for P7646, and it's actually 33419a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have misspoken whatever it is, it's hereby accurately now on the transcript. Is it ... well, it's now still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct anyhow. We take an early break and we resume at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we resume, has the Chamber understood well that there are no other witnesses available until the start of the videolink on Thursday, which was scheduled for 2.00 in the afternoon. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some concerns about that, because that's a whole day lost tomorrow where we could have heard evidence, and also for Thursday morning if the videolink is scheduled for three or three and a half hours then we would still have time to hear other evidence perhaps in the morning hours, but we'll consider how to proceed. But, of course, if there's no witness, there's no witness, but how we'll deal with the time lost, we'll consider that. Mr. Traldi, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Just one more brief transcript matter. At transcript page 59, line 7 in the temporary transcript and it was in private session but I don't think this change would necessitate going back in, I was recorded to refer to Exhibit P2725, and had intended to refer to P7275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the next one being P7276, two sequential exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby corrected. Mr. Traldi, any time estimate I mean, if we have no witnesses tomorrow it would mean that we don't conclude today it might mean that we have to come back for ten minutes or half an hour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic and I spoke about how much time each of us respectively need, and based on our calculations, it's possible we would run until 2.20 or 2.25 today. If everyone was willing to do that, everyone, including the witness, would be free of court responsibilities tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if we move forward and that's best done by focussing on the question, then there's a fair chance that we could conclude today. Otherwise we would like to see you back tomorrow for only a very short session which may not be very attractive neither for you nor for the parties or the Bench. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 80 in the English, 85 in the B/C/S, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is part of the 34th session of the Republika Srpska Assembly. Did you review this session?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we see here part of Dr. Karadzic's remarks and he says, among other things: "We have preserved," and it's about ten lines up from the bottom in the English: "We have preserved 250.000 places of the living space where Muslims used to live." Now what we just saw before the break in the Zvornik [sic] before the war 50/50 after the war the same number of people but all Serbs, that's one illustration of what was done with those preserved living space, moving Serbs in; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is unclear. What does this mean? 250.000 places living space where Muslims lived. I'm not sure I understood what that meant. What does that mean? 500, 600 Serbs south of Bihac, that's all. What is this 250.000 places? Is it settlements? Is it what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you, like we just saw in Zvornik, RS policy, Republika Srpska policy, was to move Serbs into the living spaces that Muslims had used to live in, that had been abandoned by their previous residents because of the war and the crimes that had been committed against them. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I ask that this page be added to Exhibit P2508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you uploaded in that same document including this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then we'll wait for it to be uploaded and then we'll decide on the replacement of P2508 by the newly uploaded version. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 33286.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is one more exchange list, detainees from Trnovo, Kalinovik, Gacko, Foca, Nevesinje and other places who it says were exchanged with Kalinovik. If you look, just for instance, at number 1, that's a Muslim woman's name; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now Kalinovik is -- where's Kalinovik relative to the Neretva river?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, a geography-related question. How do I put this? It is east of the Neretva river. It's a very well-known place. Several great men were born there in the Kalinovik area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what we see here again is the detention of civilians in the area covered this time by strategic objective 4, control over the Neretva; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of civilians of Muslim ethnicity, yes. Strategic objective number 4 does not refer to detention, et cetera, so this is not the result of any policy. It doesn't have to be linked to what we read in relation to those strategic objectives. We have a list here, and anybody who knows how to read can read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33490.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this is a certification from the RS MUP, dated 13 September 1993. Djordjislav Askraba, a RS MUP employee, had worked at the Kalinovik public security station and then, as agreed, the Kalinovik military command, he transferred to work in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we have the second page, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the second period, second paragraph, we read from 7 July to 7 August 1992 with the consent of the SJB, Djordjislav Askraba, police employee, was seconded to the Army of Republika Srpska, to duties and tasks of commander of the detail for providing security for detained persons of Muslim ethnicity. So this shows again the VRS is detaining civilians in -- in the geographic region covered by strategic objective 4; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer is yes because that is what it written here. But do allow me to say that it is obvious that you are basing your questions to me on those strategic objectives of Republika Srpska that we discussed yesterday. I mean, all the time we are providing illustrations for the implementations of these strategic objectives. I think it is necessary for us to see what General Mladic himself says about these strategic objectives. I have that here and I can read it out to you if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, leave it to the parties to ask you questions. You've written your report. You wait for the questions and then you answer them. And what else we need is for the parties and for this Chamber to decide. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender the last two documents, 33286 and 33490.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibits P7747 and P7748 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to step back. I'm going to try to do it very briefly, to some of your evidence about the relationship between the Serb authorities in BiH and the JNA before the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 17258.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, what we see here is a request by the RS Assembly to the JNA dated the 11th of December, 1991. At point 1, we see a -- we see a reference, first to using all available means to protect the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina as integral parts of the state of Yugoslavia, and then that the assembly is requesting -- or the assembly is referring to its decision on the territories of municipalities, local communes and populated places in Bosnia and Herzegovina which are considered the territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia. Now, this is the request you refer to on page 79 of the B/C/S, 60 of the English of D1369 that you say is a call to protect BH from internal and external enemies, including Croatian and Muslim paramilitaries; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 79 you said of this report? 79?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. No, that's not on page 79. I have to say that. It's not that page. Could you please check. I have my text printed here. It's the text about the report of Robert Donia; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we discussed earlier that the page numbers in the version we initially received had changed and I hadn't accounted for that. If you could look at the middle of page 82 in the B/C/S, I think you'll find the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And English, the page, I'm confident, remains the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, yes, I found it. Yes. "JNA to carry out its constitutional obligation and defend Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of Yugoslavia from all external and internal enemies." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, could we please have 65 ter 17179.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is another document sent to the chief of the Main Staff of the SFRY armed forces and the commanders of the 2nd and 4th Military Districts. We read at the top that: "Due to the hard-core position of the ... Croatian and Muslim peoples to separate from Yugoslavia, representatives of the Serbian nation in BH," and describes actions forming the RS offering to confederalise BH. And the second paragraph says the RS Assembly is "firmly determined to institutionalise peacefully and legally the remaining Serbian territories of BH within Yugoslavia. Therefore, in accordance with the decision to proclaim a republic, organs of authority have been formed on all levels; they will soon establish full control on the territory of Republika Srpska of BH." Now you don't mention this request in your report, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't even have the date here. I would appreciate it if you could tell me, you didn't mention it at all, and that is very important. A moment ago, it was December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we can say on the basis of discussions in the RS Assembly including comments by Dragan Kalinic at the 6th session reflected at Dr. Donia's highlight 151 in his report, that this would have followed on discussions held on the 26th of January, 1992. We can see, if we turn to the end of the document, page 3. That's in the English but we'll need to go back to page 2 in the B/C/S. Just above the words "organs of Republika Srpska," the deadline for carrying out certain tasks is 25 February. So we can say contextually it must be between 26 January and 25 February that this document was sent. Does that assist you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Here, we can already hint at what period the document is from. A moment ago I pointed out that the Assembly of the Serb People of Bosnia-Herzegovina is asking the JNA to carry out its constitutional obligation, that is to say, Article 240, Robert Donia is writing about that himself. And what it says there is that they are asking the army to defend the constitutional order of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is, in this one, which you don't refer to, what they are saying is give us guns and help us establish Serb authority. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: War is starting, everybody is being armed. Everybody is saying give us weapons. Some people are asking the JNA for weapons. Some are asking Germany. I quote that in one text. When General Blagoje Adzic says that Croat units have German weapons. So here it is the JNA that is being requested to defend the constitutional order of the country that still exists. And I don't see what is in dispute there. I could have mentioned this document as well. It would have only reinforced my own thesis. Thank you for having drawn my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I tender the last two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 17258 will be P7449. And 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter 17179 would be Exhibit P7750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7749 and P7750 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we can go back to the previous page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At point 9 we read the assembly asking for "urgent deployment of a JNA unit of adequate strength to the Kljuc municipality." We see lower down a reference to the forest location of Laniste. Now, turning to the top again of page 3 in the English, we see that the deadline for carrying out tasks 5 through 8 is 25 February, task 9 whenever possible. Now, in that regard, could we have P352, page 122. And that will be the English and B/C/S transcript. Now, here we see General Mladic's notes of a meeting on the 26th of March, 1992. Turning to page 130, we see notes on reporting on the preparations of units for relocation to new locations. Turning to page 136, for the 594th Engineering Regiment of the then-9th Corps of the JNA, he is noting the possibility of moving it to a place called Laniste. And so Mladic is helping or discussing helping fulfilling the RS Assembly request here; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Mladic is carrying out his constitutional duty. At that moment Yugoslavia is still in existence. Bosnia-Herzegovina hadn't even declared independence at that point in time, as I've already said, the constitution, Article 240, requires the army to defend the constitutional order of the country. So General Mladic is carrying out his duty here. At that moment, from a formal and legal point of view, Bosnia-Herzegovina is part of Yugoslavia. It exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 19650.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is the transcript of a speech by President Karadzic to the Herzegovina Corps on the 13th of May, 1995. Now, Karadzic is discussing negotiations. He discusses the Contact Group Plan, discusses the ambition of the West. But he also says during the course of the speech that the Bosnian Serbs inherited a lot of things in JNA storehouses dispersed a lot from the territories under the control of Croats and Muslims. That's an accurate reflection of the co-operation between the JNA and the Bosnian Serb authorities in arming what would become the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please indicate that section to me? Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have it -- I don't have the right page -- sorry. Page 6 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S, second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This big paragraph, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. And we're looking --

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. This is a completely different page from the one we looked at a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He says, "It is a fact of the matter that we inherited a lot of things in the JNA storehouses. We managed to disperse a lot of things thanks to General Kovacevic who was a colonel at the time and with the agreement between Krajisnik, myself, and General Mladic, we managed to disperse a lot of things from the territories under the control of Croats and Muslims. That is how we inherited these things." And that's a reflection, again, co-operation between the JNA and the Bosnian Serb leadership in arming Bosnian Serb forces, particularly the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is only partially yes because at that moment, Muslim and Croat forces were shooting at the JNA. When the Serbs received those weapons, the Yugoslav People's Army was under attack from Muslim and Croat forces. So would the JNA have to give weapons to those shooting at it? I wrote that in my report. The JNA was trying to call up Croat and Muslim conscripts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness, you're invited to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you resume from where why you said the JNA was trying to call up Croat and Muslim conscripts and resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see this -- okay. No, no, it's all right. No. No. Yeah. Yeah. [Interpretation] When I'm talking I follow what is written in the LiveNote and I didn't have it now. So I said that call-ups were sent by the JNA to Muslim and Croat conscripts regularly but they did not respond. Instead, party-based armies were formed that attacked the Yugoslav People's Army. What was the JNA supposed to do at that moment? It was defending itself. So I am not denying that part of the weapons that the JNA had ended up in Serb hands. That's what you asked me. But just take into account the situation. The JNA could not give weapons to those who were then shooting at it. It just couldn't be expected. It's the real situation, as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that this speech be marked and we'll make a selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you reserve a number for an excerpt still to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 19650 will be P7752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's marked for identification or, as a matter of fact, it's reserved for the excerpt to be uploaded. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart now to play a video 65 ter 27978c starting at 58 seconds. For the booth, this will be where Mr. Stanic starts speaking. And we've had it confirmed so it will only be necessary to play it once.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you give us a moment to find this transcript, please. We have different numbers not the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the interpreters' booth tell us when they are ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll now look at the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] The atmosphere is Srbinje was magnificent today. A rally that brought together several thousand people from this town and the neighbouring municipalities was held in support of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, President of Republika Srpska, and General Ratko Mladic, the army chief of Republika Srpska, the Chief of Staff of the VRS. The rally was held with the slogan, We won't give you our Nemanjics without bloodshed, and it was aimed against the provision of The Hague Tribunal which had charged them for alleged war crimes. The rally was organised by the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. Besides the representatives of the Srbinje municipality, the following people attended the rally: Zoran Vujanovic, deputy president of the Serbian Democratic Party of Republika Srpska, Bozidar Vucurevic, mayor of the Trebinje municipality, Mirko Mijatovic, deputy in the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, Dr. Dusko Kornjaca, mayor of the Cajnice municipality, Drago Pejovic, deputy in the National Assembly from Cajnice and others. Miroslav Stanic, president of the SDS Municipal Board in Srbinje was the first to greet the participants and the people of Srbinje and the neighbouring municipalities. "Stanic speech: Dear brothers and sisters, dear guests, I would like to greet you all with a sincere wish that there be no more war, but with a firm resolution that we shall be the creators of our own happiness and our own future. The young people do not remember, but those of us who are somewhat older and who -- and those who are really old here know very well that we used to organise meetings and rallies in support of Patrice Lumumba, Che Guevara, the Carinthian Slovenes, the Czechoslovakians, the Khmer Rouge and many others whose names are now almost unpronounceable. So why not support ourselves today? We want to choose our own leaders for ourselves. We, the Serbs living to the west of the Drina river, know very well that our leaders are Dr. Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic. We do not care much who the president of the Muslim Croatian Federation will be and even less of America or Russia. We know that the local people there, the local voters, will decide that. Why should then others make decisions here for us? My personal opinion about this unprecedented international hunt for our leaders is well known but I hope that other participants will present this even better. In the name of justice, in the name of democracy, in the name of your will, the will of the people, I greet you all once again."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I'm a bit puzzled. It was supposed to start and -- the speech would start but we heard a lot of comment before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think I probably expressed myself unclearly and so we did get the introduction but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's done now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, what Mr. Stanic says -- so two questions. First, he is referred to as the president of the Municipal Board in Srbinje. That had previously been called Foca which we talked about before; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Foca is an old medieval name for this town which was part of the Serbian state in the Middle Ages. It was a mistake to change that name. It was an ancient town. It was part of the Serbian state. It was a mistake to change the name of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when he says we the Serbs west of the Drina river know our leaders are Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, that's an accurate reflection of Mladic as well as Karadzic's power and responsibility in Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked you more than once to be clear about the date. Again, you haven't told me when this happened to see whether at this time they were the responsible ones in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can tell you that it was during the war so Karadzic is the president and Mladic is the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's the most precise can you get? During the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't comment. You can ask, and I will ask Mr. Traldi now whether he has any further details as to the date of this speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll check our records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Are you unable to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am able to answer this question, of course, it's obvious that this gentleman recognises the authority and the powers of Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. You can hear that in his speech. You can't take anything away from it. Or add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P7753, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, could you give us a further time estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would say about 15 minutes, possibly 20, Your Honour, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to finish in 15 minutes, if possible. Mr. Stojanovic has your time estimate changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This moment, Your Honour, no. We reckon with two documents and about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P3076.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is part of the transcript of the 37th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 18 in English; 13, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the 10th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: General Mladic is speaking and he says in this long paragraph at the end: "The next thing is that this is our historical chance to create a state. Not any kind of state, but an all-Serbian state of a round shape with access to the sea and horogravske and horografske facilities, and as little enemies as possible, those who could be our potential enemies and raise against us again in a few years." Now, first, you mention in your reports and you mentioned this morning some of General Mladic's comments at the assembly. You do not mention this one; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned the comment of General Mladic from 12 May 1992. Obviously you have different statements by General Mladic. The question is which one to pick. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that say something and to do something are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, Mr. Traldi has chosen to take you to this speech. So would you please answer in that respect. I think it was the January 1994, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that's we're focussing on now. But now hopefully before you answer the question, do you have any explanation what "Horogravske" means because in the English translation, it seems to be an unknown expression. Could you assist us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leaning well on the sea, I don't know what this means. Maybe it's a military technical term that I don't know. I see it for the first time. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any of the parties could assist us. It may have got something to do with the transcription or the recording of -- because two times the word is in one line and grafske might have to do something with writing. But the witness cannot assist us. Could you now please answer the question that was put to you by Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether I put this statement in my report. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, an all-Serbian state, that's exactly what we saw happened in Rajlovac, Vogosca, and Foca; right? It was all Serb or almost entirely Serb.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. All Serb does not mean that in that Serbian state there would be no Serbs [as interpreted]. That's not correct. The leadership of Republika Srpska and General Mladic want the preservation of a multi-ethnic Yugoslavia. That is rejected. Secession occurs and now in Sarajevo, Alija Izetbegovic -- my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also check the transcript in English page 85, line 20, sounds a bit illogical. I don't know whether the witness made a mistake or, but would you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, first, you said all Serb does not mean in that Serbian state and you were recorded to say there would be no Serbs. Did you mean to say it doesn't mean there will be no non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes I'll repeat. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want a specific answer. It doesn't imply that in these territories there would be no non-Serbs. It only means the democratic right of the Serbian people to self-determination, as required by all the other Yugoslav peoples, and which is a completely legitimate right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm interested in focussing on these particular remarks. So when Mladic says this all-Serbian state will have, among other things, as little enemies as possible, those who could be our potential enemies and raise against us in a few years, who do you understand him to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Newly formed states in the territory of Yugoslavia for which General Mladic fought like all the other leaders of Republika Srpska are fragmented. Look at the borders even today, the borders created --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after the breakup --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the limitation of borders. Who do you understand him to mean when he says "as few enemies as possible"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do I mean -- who does he mean? I'm a historian, I'm not a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If you look at the end of the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see that the witness thinks that as a historian he -- where he can't answer the question so then we accept that he can't do that because he is a historian and unable then to interpret any texts. Well, let's then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the next paragraph at the end, sir, General Mladic says: "We have to understand that Muslims and Croats who are like this represent a danger by this knife." Does that assist you as a historian in figuring out who he meant were the enemies?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. Is that in the next paragraph? I can't see that passage. Must be on the next page in B/C/S. If you could just point it out to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it was just at the end of the previous page. We have now moved to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Look at the last line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Uh-huh. Very well. Of course, this is not about Muslims and Croats here, not the Muslims and Croats who remain within the borders of that Serbian state. It could refer equally to those who stayed outside in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, in the territories controlled by the Muslims. The whole debate was about the Serbs' desire for a multi-ethnic state in Yugoslavia and the Muslim leadership rejected that and they wanted their own unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "the whole debate," you're not talking about a debate at the 37th session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, you're talking about a debate in January, February, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not discussed at this session of the assembly but it remains a topic for historians to this day; what did Serbs want? This is January 1992 -- 1994. It's been years into the war. Serbs are again working for separation. That's the first war objective. They had lost their illusions about the possibility to live in that state, and they have a democratic right to choose what they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally can we have P431.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. You refer to several of General Mladic's comments at this session in your report. Can we have page 34 in the English and 33 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 12th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The 12th of May, 1992 is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: General Mladic says here, about ten lines down from the top in the English, "Please, let not only put our minds into what we are doing but also think thoroughly about it and let us be cautious about when to keep mum. No, the thing that we are doing, needs to be guarded as our deepest secret." If what Mladic was talking about at this assembly session was, as you said, peace and living together, that wouldn't have needed to be kept secret, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Anyone who has served in the army knows there are secrets which are not discussed in the army. General Mladic is a general of the Serb army. There are things that are not talked about. It's part of the war. Anyone who did his military service knows that. General Mladic functions as a soldier. Please allow me in my answer to this question to read out what Mladic said on 12 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a short passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, please focus on the passage we're discussing. Mladic next says: "What our representatives appearing in the media at political talks and negotiations are going to say, and they do need to present our goals in a way that will sound appealing to the ears" --

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, just could you show me where it is. I can't see the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you not interrupt Mr. Traldi when he is putting a question to you. Rather, listen to what he reads. But since we're interrupted anyhow now, Mr. Traldi, if you could find the portion in B/C/S so as to accommodate the witness, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my Cyrillic is not the strongest, and so it's taking me a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if could you assist, or Mr. Ivetic, that would be appreciated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just looking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just show me in English and then I'll find it more easily in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's about ten lines down in the English. You see a line saying starting with the word "republic," and it's about three lines down to the right, starting: "And please ..."

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems it's not here. Not on this page. There's no mention of Republika Srpska Krajina. Maybe the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I see, Mr. Traldi, it may not be on this page because reference to numbers often help me. I see in the English not the 10.000, neither do I see in the B/C/S the numbers 650 kilometres and 150 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I take the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, to facilitate letting you go home, I'm just going to put to you the evidence the Chamber has received, if that works for everybody. Which is what we have in the English, which is General Mladic describing what's being done at this assembly as the deepest secret, saying that what our representatives appearing at political talks and negotiations are going to say has to be presented in a way that will sound appealing and that our people must know how to read between the lines. Now, that wouldn't be necessary unless what they were talking about doing was something criminal; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Every army, every country has things that are not publicly discussed. It doesn't have to be criminal. Why would we conclude that it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this is discussion is not taking place in the army. It's taking place in the RS Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? Of course. These are the highest state bodies of Republika Srpska. All parliaments of the world have something called closed session. Are you going to accuse them that they are discussing crimes? Unless have you a negative bias towards a given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... closed session, he is just telling them in a public session that they must keep some things secret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer to this question is no. That is not implied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but my recollection of the evidence that the Chamber has received is that this is also a closed session of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that is so, then thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber has also received evidence, it has the whole speech. You quote Mladic saying: "Therefore, we cannot cleanse" - it's on page 35 in the English - "nor can we have a sieve to sift so that only Serbs would stay, or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest would leave." Now, you refer to this part in your report. The Chamber has received evidence that he continues as we see: "Well, that is, that will not, I do not know how Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic would explain this to the world." So he is, again, expressing concern about public reaction in that comment; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It requires a major effort to follow this because we don't have the Serbian text, so I'm listening to the interpretation and following the English text. But I will try to answer. At this session, it's the 12th of May, 1992, if I'm not mistaken in Banja Luka, General Mladic is speaking as a reasonable man who is warning of all the problems and troubles that are there. If you will not give me an opportunity to read out what he said, and I did not refer to this in my report, didn't find it in Dr. Donia's report, if this is evidence for the indictment, then what did General Mladic say that cannot be included in the indictment? I'm drawing your attention to 16 through 18, these are statements of General Mladic at this session and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, again, it may be it's already in evidence. You don't know. I have no clear recollection. We leave it to the parties and you were called by the Defence so whatever was important, the Defence could have asked you either in the examination-in-chief or to include that in the report. So, therefore, leave it to them, and don't seek to impose upon us what we should hear from you because you consider it to be relevant and important. Mr. Mladic is seeking for a -- but he first should sit down. And meanwhile, we'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You apparently do not understand the structure of criminal proceedings, Witness, that's a pity. Because it takes a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I understand that very well. You do not wish to hear what General Mladic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we wish to hear what the parties, including the Defence who called you as a witness to whatever. I mean, this Chamber is open to everything. But it is the parties and the Chamber who will consider what is relevant or not and not for you to decide at this moment. Mr. Traldi, any further questions, because we are ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just one final one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we've seen Mladic call at the assembly calling for an all-Serbian state. We've seen municipality after municipality that had become ethnically all-Serb. Is it your conclusion as a historian that that's somehow a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you put that question more clearly. I didn't understand it. What is a mere coincidence? I will be happy to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That municipality after municipality in the Republika Srpska had become, by population, 99 or 100 per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We saw him call for an all-Serb state. We saw that happen in a bunch of municipalities on the ground. Is it your evidence that that's somehow a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's hard to answer this question. It is suggestive. I can give a more extensive answer. It has to do with the democratic will of the Serb people. I mean, it doesn't have to be a coincidence, and it may be a coincidence. However, your question already implies answer. What does coincidence mean? Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina are struggling for self-determination and for the creation of a Serb state. They are not struggling for ethnically pure territories. No. They fought for a multi-ethnic Yugoslavia. It is the 12th of May. Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as independent so war only started, if we're talking about this session. So Serbs are struggling for a multi-ethnic Yugoslavia. That Serb state could not have been without minorities. That is what they struggled for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few, Your Honours. Could we please have P7725 in e-court. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The document that you were cross-examined on during my colleague's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you say -- thank you. It's corrected on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, Professor Kovic, there was a question that had to do with what happened in Kijevo. And at one point, on page 3 of today's transcript, you said that: "If necessary, I can explain in greater detail what it was that happened in Kijevo." I would kindly ask you to tell the Trial Chamber why you felt it was necessary to say something like that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report of Robert Donia, the importance of Kijevo is insisted upon as a turning point in the activity of the JNA and General Mladic himself. Purportedly after that, the JNA started attacking, not only protecting. If that were true, General Kukanjac would have razed Sarajevo to the ground. The JNA in Sarajevo and all the attacks and humiliations against the JNA, what happened after Kijevo show that Kijevo is of no significance, no special significance. General Ninkovic was commander there, not General Mladic. He carried out his duty there. And, number three -- Spiro Ninkovic, that is. So it is the month of August 1991, the JNA is being fired at from all conceivable weaponry. I already said that Vladimir Seks had ordered an all-out attack against the JNA, so you have an armed force that is defending itself in its own territory and defending the constitutional order of that country, and that is it's constitutional duty. That is what I wished to say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked not to speak that closely into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you stay a little bit away from the microphone. Not that much but to -- not coming too close. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P7729.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the cross-examination today, you were asked about this document, Professor Kovic. As can you see here, the date is the 8th of April, 1992. Let us please focus on paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, in English, could we please move onto the next page and look at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the second subparagraph, it says: "During the afternoon, mortar fire was opened on the sector of Vratnik and the old part of the city of Sarajevo by the members of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Pale. After the intervention of the command of the 2nd Military District, the fire stopped soon." This is my question: April 1992, the TO, what does that mean? And under whose command is the TO in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: TO is Territorial Defence. It is very important because Territorial Defences primarily in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina - but also in the Republic of Croatia - became the nucleus of the armed unlawful units so the Muslim and Croat forces grew out of that. This document shows that the army - and it's General Kukanjac, he is the commander of the 2nd District - he is separating the parties. The Prosecution is trying to prove through this that the Serbs were firing at the city. And it is the 8th of April, and the JNA is separating the forces and fire is opened at the JNA in the territory of Sarajevo. General Kukanjac as Alija Izetbegovic said on that day, when he was taken prisoner and the day he spent at General Kukanjac's, it was the 3rd of May, he said that he saw tanks that the general could use to destroy the entire town and he never did that. That is the role of General Kukanjac. And that is almost a year after Kijevo. That is the situation in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please stay away from the microphone, not come that close, and could he please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are again invited not to come too close to the microphone and also to slow down your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to answer the last question which you didn't do. Under whose command is the TO, the Territorial Defence, in April 1992. Short answer, please. That was the answer of Mr. Stojanovic. That was the question of Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give a precise answer to that question because Territorial Defences were disintegrating into individual fragments. It was certain that they were not under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P7728 in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, it's that intercept that you were asked about today. The date is the 21st of April, 1992. According to this typewritten text, it is a conversation between Goran Saric and Mico Davidovic. Judging by the names of these persons, could you try to assume - unless you know them personally - what ethnic community they belong to, what people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by their names and surnames, they're probably ethnic Serbs, although in our part of the world, sometimes it is a bit difficult to tell. Davidovic, Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move onto the next page both in B/C/S and in English?

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me. Davidovic is a frequent Serb last name. Saric, not exactly. But it's very hard to say what the exact ethnic background will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS KOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you follow this conversation, if this is the way it was, Goran Saric says to Mico Davidovic: "Well, for the time being, that's why I am, fuck, I actually do nothing, and currently I cannot leave Sarajevo."
